action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. ## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

1	# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)
2	
3	Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.
4	
5	## Schema
6	
7	Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.
8	
9	Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.
10	
11	## Voices: label every one
12	
13	- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
14	- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
15	- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
16	- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.
17	
18	## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)
19	
20	- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
21	- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
22	- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
23	- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
24	- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.
25	
26	## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)
27	
28	- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
29	- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
30	- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
31	- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
32	- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
33	- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
34	- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.
35	
36	## Evidence
37	
38	- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
39	- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
40	- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
41	- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.
42	
43	## Confidence
44	
45	- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
46	- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).
47	
48	## Dedup and converge
49	
50	Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.
51	
52	## Baylor context
53	
54	Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.
55	
56	## Scope and output
57	
58	- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
59	- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
60	- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.
61

1	---
2	name: ingest-book
3	description: >-
4	  Ingest a book (PDF/EPUB full-text, Kindle highlights, or framework-only from a
5	  physical book) into the SecondBrain library as atomized, citable advisor entries. Use
6	  when the user wants to "ingest a book", "add a book to my library/advisors",
7	  "/ingest-book", or points at a book file for the advisor system. Do not use for
8	  articles, transcripts, or general resources (use ingest-resource).
9	argument-hint: "[book file or title] [domain]"
10	---
11	
12	# Ingest Book
13	
14	Turn a book into atomized, citable entries under the library subtree, grouped by domain and book, ready for the `advisor` skill.
15	
16	**Library root:** `vault_library` in the selected platform config
17	**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` (`vault_library`, `vault_root`) — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.
18	**Extractors:** `~/.claude/skills/ingest-book/lib/extract_epub.py`, `extract_pdf.py`
19	Run extractors inside the context-mode sandbox (`ctx_execute`, language python) so raw book text never enters the conversation — only the atomized entries you write do.
20	
21	## Model split (cost vs quality)
22	
23	This skill mixes three kinds of work with very different model needs:
24	- **Extraction & structure mapping** (probe, chapter map, text cleanup) — deterministic
25	  Python in the sandbox. **Zero model tokens; model choice irrelevant.**
26	- **Orchestration** (searches, `_book.md` updates, dedup checks) — mechanical.
27	  **Haiku-tier is fine.**
28	- **Atomization** (Phase 2/3: distilling prose into accurate entries with correct
29	  mechanism-vs-claim, honest confidence, and a real "when NOT to apply") — this is where
30	  the advisor's entire value is created. **Run on Sonnet or stronger. Do NOT use Haiku
31	  for atomization** — a weak distillation becomes a permanent low-quality entry, and the
32	  generated output is only ~3K tokens/chapter, so quality-per-token matters far more than
33	  price-per-token. Cost levers that DON'T hurt quality: atomize only chapters you'll
34	  consult, and checkpoint + `/clear` between chapter batches (see Rules) so context
35	  doesn't compound across the book.
36	
37	## Schema for every entry note
38	
39	Filename: `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md`, `kind ∈ {principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim}`.
40	
41	```yaml
42	---
43	type: library-entry
44	kind: principle
45	domain: <domain-slug>
46	book: <book-slug>
47	chapter: "N"            # or section label; "" if highlights with no location
48	topic: <2-5 word topic>
49	category: [tag, tag]
50	confidence: proven      # proven | supported | untested | contested
51	ingest-tier: full-text  # full-text | highlights | framework-only
52	created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
53	---
54	
55	# <Human title of the idea>
56	
57	**What it is** — one tight paragraph.
58	**Why it works** — mechanism, not restatement.
59	**When to apply** — concrete triggers.
60	**When NOT to apply** — scope limits. (MANDATORY — never omit.)
61	**Example** — one concrete instance.
62	```
63	
64	**Confidence is bounded by tier:** full-text ≤ proven; highlights ≤ supported;
65	framework-only ≤ untested. Set `contested` by hand when sources conflict.
66	
67	## Phase 1 — Intake
68	
69	1. Identify: book title, author, source type (PDF/EPUB | Kindle highlights | physical), target domain.
70	2. Compute `<book-slug>` = `kebab(title)--kebab(lastname)` (e.g. `supertraining--verkhoshansky`).
71	3. If the domain folder/`_domain.md` doesn't exist, create them (mirror the S&C `_domain.md` format).
72	4. Build `_book.md` chapter map:
73	   - EPUB/PDF: run the extractor with `--list` / `--probe` to get the chapter or page structure.
74	   - Physical: ask the user for the chapter list, or assemble from a verified public listing.
75	   Write `_book.md` (template below) with every chapter `status: pending`.
76	
77	`_book.md` template:
78	```markdown
79	---
80	type: book-index
81	book: <book-slug>
82	title: <full title>
83	author: <author>
84	domain: <domain-slug>
85	ingest-tier: full-text | highlights | framework-only
86	source: "<file path or 'physical' or 'kindle-highlights'>"
87	created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
88	---
89	
90	# <title> — ingest map
91	
92	| # | Chapter | Status | Entries |
93	|---|---------|--------|---------|
94	| 0 | <title> | pending | 0 |
95	```
96	
97	## Phase 2 — Extract (by tier)
98	
99	**Full-text (PDF/EPUB):**
100	- First run `extract_pdf.py --probe`. If `scanned: true`, STOP the full-text path:
101	  tell the user the PDF is image-only, and fall back to framework-only tier (set
102	  `ingest-tier: framework-only`, cap confidence at untested). Never emit full-text-
103	  confidence entries from a scanned file.
104	- Work **one chapter at a time** (EPUB `--chapter N`; PDF `--pages A-B`, where A and B are
105	  0-based PDF indexes and the range is inclusive: `--pages 12-20` returns 9 pages). Each page
106	  comes back with `page` (0-based index) and `viewer_page` (what a PDF viewer shows, index + 1).
107	  Cite pages one way throughout a book and state the convention in `_book.md`. For each:
108	  extract candidate ideas → atomize per the schema → write entry notes.
109	- **After each chapter**, update that row in `_book.md` to `status: done` with the
110	  entry count. This is the resume checkpoint — never batch this update.
111	
112	**Kindle highlights:**
113	- Parse `My Clippings.txt` or the highlights export in the sandbox. Cluster highlights
114	  by theme; write one entry per theme. `ingest-tier: highlights`, confidence ≤ supported.
115	- Attribute `chapter` from the highlight's location metadata when present, else "".
116	
117	**Framework-only (physical / scanned):**
118	- Briefly interview the user for their takeaways. Supplement with *verified* public
119	  chapter summaries. Write 5–15 framework-level entries. `ingest-tier: framework-only`,
120	  confidence ≤ untested.
121	
122	## Phase 3 — Quality gate (run before writing each batch)
123	
124	- One idea per note. If an extracted point is compound, split it.
125	- "When NOT to apply" present and non-trivial.
126	- **Dedup + converge:** before writing, `memsearch search` the library for the same
127	  concept. If an existing entry (any book) covers it, DON'T duplicate — instead add a
128	  `[[wikilink]]` + one line to both notes recording the agreement, and only add a new
129	  note if it contributes a genuinely new angle.
130	- Never overwrite an existing file; on slug collision append `-2`.
131	
132	## Phase 4 — Close-out
133	
134	1. Set all done rows in `_book.md`; if partial, leave pending rows for next session.
135	2. Add the book to `_domain.md`'s `books:` list and the "Books in this domain" section.
136	3. Add the book-slug to the advisor persona's `books:` list (`advisors/<domain>.md`)
137	   if an advisor exists.
138	4. Run `memsearch index "<vault_library>"` using the selected platform config
139	   so entries are searchable immediately (don't wait for the SessionEnd hook).
140	5. Commit the vault using `vault_root` from the selected platform config: `git -C "<vault_root>" add Knowledge/library && git commit -m "ingest(<book-slug>): <N> entries, ch X-Y"`.
141	6. Report: entries by kind and confidence, links created, chapters remaining.
142	
143	## Rules
144	- Raw book text stays in the sandbox; only atomized entries enter context/the vault.
145	- Resumable by design: `_book.md` is the source of truth for "where am I".
146	- A 300-page book is a multi-session job — stop at a chapter boundary, never mid-chapter.
147

1	# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)
2	
3	Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26. Revised 2026-09-28 with Eric's method interview (`docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`, 30 of 30 answered).
4	
5	## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)
6	
7	Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:
8	
9	- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
10	- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
11	- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
12	  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
13	- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.
14	
15	Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).
16	
17	Tags added 2026-09-28 from the method interview:
18	
19	- **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric stated or claimed the position in the interview. His words are quoted as "Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Qn):". Q1 claimed exactly four course positions (Vermeil hierarchy, undulating periodization, Dynamic Correspondence, the football energy-system priority stack); other course material stays Inferred.
20	- **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric said the source or practice is not current. The old content is kept and marked, not deleted, so a synthesis note can see what changed.
21	- **Superseded by interview (Qn)**: a documented position, sometimes from Eric's own slides, that his interview answer replaces.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Philosophy and decision principles
26	
27	- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
28	- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
29	- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]

141	- Bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk in its own right: an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
142	- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
143	- No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; the detailed treatment of ACWR and injury-risk modeling that does exist (Clemson curriculum) is reference material only, not confirmed Baylor practice. Confirmed by the interview: there is no formal risk model.
144	- ACWR is looked at but not trusted for any decision. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12): "We dabble with ACWR but I don't personally trust it for anything. I think it's raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally. We don't have any formal risk model that we follow. We've avoided them up to this point, but there's not a really good reason why." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q12)**
145	- Movement screens are collected and filed, not used to change programs. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12): "there isn't anything that changes decisions made to a program; it's more or less just collected and referred to for future needs." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q12)** Inference: this sits uneasily with his own Q3 rule; see Tension 15.
146	
147	*Thin discipline, now answered: the finding is that nothing formal exists (no risk model, ACWR distrusted, screens not acted on).*
148	
149	## Recovery and sleep
150	
151	- Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9]
152	- Recovery appears in the department's own subcategory list of Athletic Performance (alongside strength, conditioning, speed, agility, power, nutrition, applied performance, sports psychology, RTP), but no specific recovery protocol, sleep target, or monitoring tool is described anywhere in this corpus. **Explicit (named as a subcategory) / gap (no protocol stated)** [week1-lecture.md p.11]
153	- Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q23): "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)**
154	
155	*Thin discipline, now answered: the finding is that nothing formal exists beyond load design.*
156	
157	## Nutrition and body composition
158	
159	- Performance Nutrition is explicitly a separate Health & Wellness unit from Applied Performance, owning individual nutrition consultations, supplement education, body composition and bone density assessment, and the training table/fueling stations. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.5]
160	- Body composition testing is capped at no more than 4 times per year. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Anthropometrics"]
161	- Anthropometrics (height, weight, muscle-to-fat ratio) are described as strongly associated with success in most sports and worth tracking even though they are owned by Performance Nutrition rather than Applied Performance. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Anthropometrics"]
162	- No nutrition decision rules, body-composition targets, or thresholds are attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; this appears to be a deliberate department-design choice (Performance Nutrition owns it) rather than an oversight.
163	- No force-plate or GPS data flows to Performance Nutrition; bodyweight is consulted only when there is a problem. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q24): "It does not. Only if there is an issue will bodyweight be consulted. Nothing proactive." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q24)**
164	
165	*Thin discipline, now answered: the finding is that there is no proactive data link between Applied Performance and Performance Nutrition.*

167	## Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach
168	
169	- A trained "coach's eye," built through repetition and attention, is treated as at least as important as any technology for daily assessment: "you don't need a fancy test or anything to do that. But you do have to have a good coach's eye." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.8] Eric's own position (interview 2026-09-28, Q6) is narrower: the eye tells you where to look, and data then investigates. See the Philosophy bullet and Tension 3.
170	- Constraints-led and external-cue coaching are not part of Eric's practice. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q25): "I don't apply it, as I don't fully understand it. I want to know more." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q25)** A learning request, a candidate for a primer.
171	- New movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3-4 weeks of practice to become efficient and low-energy-cost, which informs how much proficiency to expect when a new exercise or drill is introduced. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.6-7]
172	- Movement efficiency (skill) is treated as directly reducing energy cost — elite athletes (cited examples: LeBron James, Deion Sanders) are described as outlasting and outperforming peers partly through tactical efficiency that lowers the physical output required to achieve the same result. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.8-9]
173	- Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced, on the observed premise that many incoming athletes have high sport-specific skill from early specialization but poor general movement competency. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
174	
175	*Still thin. The interview added the coach's-eye rule (Q6) and confirmed that constraints-led coaching is not in use (Q25). The rest of this section is shared course material, unclaimed.*
176	
177	## Periodization and programming
178	
179	- Macro/meso/microcycle structure is used as the standard planning language, with an explicit reminder that a "training week" does not have to equal 7 calendar days — it can be extended to fit training themes around a real competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.17-18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
180	- The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume), before a transition into competition. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]
181	- In-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity even when the practice schedule looks repetitive week to week, specifically to avoid training monotony for the athlete. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21]
182	- Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block — "you can't ride two horses with one saddle." Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29; week1-lecture.md p.70]
183	- An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract: lay out the competition calendar, key non-training dates (holidays, exam weeks), and phase-by-phase volume/intensity waves, then adapt the route as circumstances change while still reaching the same destination. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.22-23; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.13-15]
184	- Training residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue readiness for max-velocity work degrades. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27] Inference: these are Issurin's figures, and Eric sides with Issurin (interview 2026-09-28, Q16), so the speed half reads as his; the aerobic and strength halves were not asked directly.
185	- In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14): "in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of November as you get closer to the postseason ... That's when players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)** He did not say whether the postseason gets a distinct taper.
186	- The in-season game week: Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)**
187	- Bye weeks: three practice days, extra rest and recovery, slightly higher practice volume than a game week, a speed and strength top-up, and harder work for players with few game snaps. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q17): "guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)**
188	- The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.16]
189	
190	## Data, technology and reporting
191	
192	- The full technology stack: Catapult (GPS), Kitman Labs (central AMS/data store), Perch (camera-based velocity-based training), Polar (heart rate), and the VALD suite — DynaMo, ForceDecks, ForceFrame, Hub, NordBord, SmartSpeed. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
193	- Kitman Labs is positioned specifically as the cross-technology data store and analysis/visualization layer, distinct from each vendor's own reporting tool (e.g., VALD Hub, OpenField Cloud). **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
194	- System of record: each source system holds its own data (force data in VALD, Catapult data in OpenField), Kitman AMS aggregates, and the source system wins when Kitman disagrees. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q11): "They're separate entities; one doesn't overrule the other. If Kitman had wrong numbers from VALD or OpenField, we would go to those sources to correct it: the source systems overrule any errors Kitman made bringing data into the platform." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q11)**
195	- Documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting) except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]
196	- Credential/login management is currently placeholder-only in the Playbook; a secure credential-vault protocol is named as needed but not yet implemented. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.8; performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
197	- Standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist; building them is named as unfinished Phase 2 work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2] Who builds reports today: strength staff for most teams (interview 2026-09-28, Q28; see Department model).
198	- Tensiomyography (TMG) is part of the toolkit, with a documented setup/operations SOP, but that SOP is headed with the names of a prior Director and Associate Director of Applied Performance (Althoff, Nelson), not Eric, and current active use is unclear from this corpus. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q29)**; was Inferred (legacy document, status unclear) [technologytemplatesop.md] Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q29): "Only Chris Ruf with Track still uses it."
199	
200	## Education and staff development
201	
202	- HHPR 5355 ("Power, Speed, Agility, & Periodization in Training") is Eric's own graduate-level course, co-taught with Chris Ruf and Michael Wenger; grading is split across two exams (10% and 20%), a group training-plan project (20%), and lecture/lab participation (40%), with a practical (teach-back) component on exams. **Inferred (transcript, syllabus content)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.1]
203	- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson model to Baylor's own technology stack (ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar) and to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5] Status: a proposal only. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q30): "It has not been built yet." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q30)**
204	- Curriculum design principle: interns need both the "why" (conceptual education) and the "how" (hands-on technical training) each week, and should leave the program with a professional portfolio of real work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics), not just device-operation checklists. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1, 5.4]
205	- The proposed curriculum deliberately adds sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services, reflecting Baylor's specific department structure (Applied Performance inside Health & Wellness) rather than copying Clemson's Olympic-sports-only framing. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3]
206

209	## No material found
210	
211	None. Every one of the sixteen required sections had at least some material. Several sections are thin, though, and should be read as gaps rather than settled positions: **Rehab and return to play**, **Injury risk and prevention**, **Recovery and sleep**, **Nutrition and body composition**, and **Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach**. See `interview-prep.md`.
212	
213	Update after the interview (2026-09-28): four of the five thin sections now have an answer, and for three of them the answer is that nothing formal exists, which is itself the finding. Injury risk: no formal model, ACWR distrusted, screens not acted on (Q12). Recovery and sleep: load design only, nothing objective tracked (Q23). Nutrition: no proactive data flow (Q24). Rehab and RTP: role stated (Q4, Q22) and a written protocol exists in the UE and LE templates (Q4a), not yet staged. Coaching stays thin: constraints-led coaching is not used (Q25), and the rest is unclaimed course material.

216	
217	## Tensions and contradictions
218	
219	Status after the interview (2026-09-28): resolved 1 (partly), 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9; still open 7 (partly), 8, 10. New tensions from the interview are 11 to 16. Each entry below carries its status on its last line.
220	
221	1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.
222	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): partly resolved.** Q1 claimed four positions (Vermeil hierarchy, undulating periodization, Dynamic Correspondence, the football energy-system stack), now Explicit. Every other transcript bullet stays Inferred.
223	
224	2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.
225	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q5): "Both." Both framings are true at once.
226	
227	3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.
228	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q6): the coach's eye flags where to look; data then investigates. The two are sequential, not rival defaults.
229	
230	4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.
231	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q8): V12 "is not current"; a new manual built on the NCAA technology and sport-science recommendations is in development. All V12 bullets are marked Legacy.
232	
233	5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.
234	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved by Q8.** Inference: with V12 not current, the Force Plate Testing V3 cues govern. Eric did not address the cueing question itself.
235	
236	6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]
237	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric (Q20): "Age-based." The body-size table is marked Superseded. Note that the body-size table was from Eric's own assigned session, so his slides and his practice differ.
238	
239	7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.
240	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): still open, confirmed.** Eric (Q30): the intern curriculum "has not been built yet."
241	
242	8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.
243	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): open.** Not asked. Inference: the Q3 rule ("if it doesn't answer a question anyone has...") would retire the roster-wide SOP.
244	
245	9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.
246	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved.** Eric claimed undulating periodization (Q1).
247	
248	10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.
249	   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): open.** Not asked.
250	
251	New tensions raised by the interview (2026-09-28):
252	
253	11. **Eric's own slide against his interview on residual effects.** The class-4 slide (p. 47), from a session Eric taught, says aerobic fitness is lost fastest and speed slowest. In the interview he sides with Issurin, speed fades fastest (Q16), and says Issurin drives speed programming. The slide bullet is marked Superseded. Inference: the slide still circulates in HHPR 5355 and should be reconciled before next spring. The peaking synthesis keeps the counter-evidence both ways.
254	12. **Daily mRSI testing against a Wednesday read.** The SportSmith piece describes mRSI from daily CMJ testing as the daily readiness marker [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]. Q2 names Wednesday as the day. Inference: daily collection with one weekly decision day would reconcile them, but Eric did not say which; worth one follow-up.
255	13. **"We don't assess readiness" against mRSI as the readiness marker.** Q22 says Applied Performance does not assess readiness in RTP; the SportSmith piece and Q2 describe mRSI readiness reads. Inference: Q22 is scoped to RTP, so these probably do not conflict, but the RTP templates should be checked.
256	14. **"Support" role against "it doesn't really end".** The Playbook frames RTP input as support to Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance decisions [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]. Q4 describes ongoing testing, progression and shared loading decisions with no end point. Inference: compatible (support can be continuous), but the Playbook wording understates the role.
257	15. **The Q3 rule against current practice.** Eric's rule is that a test with no question or need has no place (Q3). Yet ACWR is still looked at ("We dabble with ACWR") though he does not "trust it for anything", and movement screens are "just collected" without changing decisions (Q12). Inference: by his own rule both are candidates to retire or to be given a question.
258	16. **No true 1RM against %1RM prescription.** No sport tests true 1RM (Q10), while Prilepin's chart and the phase bands are written in %1RM [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]. Inference: loads are percentages of projected maxes, so their error carries into every prescription. Not a contradiction in practice, but worth stating.
259	17. **DSI as a plyo-vs-strength switch against the evidence.** Eric uses DSI to choose plyometric versus max-strength emphasis (Q21). The evidence check (`docs/synthesis/_work/dsi-evidence-check.md`) finds that IMTP PF explains most of DSI's variance, that the 0.60/0.80 cutoffs were never validated, and that the one controlled trial found a benefit only in its strength arm. Inference: keep the test, but decide on CMJ PF and IMTP PF alongside the ratio, and set cutoffs from the roster.
260

# Case Study: An Elite Sprinter and a Hurdler on Run-Specific Isometrics

**What it is** — Natera presents two athletes (~93:07–101:49).

**Elite male sprinter.** He was a strong, "power-hungry" athlete: a good accelerator but poorly elastic, with a weak max velocity.
- **Baseline:** back squat about **2.65× BW**; isometric mid-thigh pull **5.78× BW**. It is unclear whether that was single- or double-leg; the pull came before Natera moved to iso squats. CMJ about **59–62 cm**.
- **GPP:** eccentric calf work, then hip ISO holds progressing to switches.
- **SPP:** ankle and hip ISO catches, plus "ISO stadium descents," a loaded, cyclical isometric step-down that comes after the continuum.
- **Loads cited:** ankle ISO catch "up to 160 kg" (the transcript says "leaving up to 160 kilo"), which is implausible against his own 60 kg example and needs verifying on video. Hip ISO catch about 35 kg.
- **Reported changes:** CMJ +3 cm; CMJ power (~6,000 W) +200–300 W; takeoff velocity up; **RSI** "improved significantly," which he calls the main win; shorter contact times at about 30–40 m; longer acceleration and higher max velocity (around 11 m/s).

**Female 100 m hurdler.** She was coached by a Polish coach whose name the ASR renders "Peter Marazu ski" (name unverified), with Natera collaborating. Her times stagnated in 2016–2017. Run-specific isometrics (RSI) were added in 2018 through mid-2019 alongside "track training" and traditional squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts. She used **holds and pushes only**, and progressed past targets such as a **2× BW ankle hold**. Afterwards her hurdle times and speed improved to "elite level." Her quote to a reporter: "I don't lift heavy weights. I just hold them."

*(Every number is single-source ASR from slides; the before/after charts are visual only. Verify at ~95:05–100:58.)*

**Why it works** — Natera's interpretation: isometrics raised reactive strength without extra plyometric volume, and position-specific strength carried over into running. Neither interpretation can be separated from other causes in these data.

**When to apply** — Use the sprinter as a **profile template**, not as evidence: high max strength (squat ≥2.5× BW) plus a low RSI and poor max velocity is the athlete Natera would target. In football that is the big, strong accelerator (RB/LB type) whose drop-jump RSI on ForceDecks is low for his strength. Track RSI and single-leg iso push together to see whether one moves without the other.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** Each case is n = 1 with concurrent training: sprint coaching, traditional lifting, technical work and maturation. There is no control, and the selection is plainly of successes. The hurdler also had a new collaborating coach, "great coaching and great technical training," per Natera himself. Elsewhere (~34:19–35:15) he reports programs where RSI was "the only change," and he concedes that is "not exactly a controlled scientific experiment." Do not cite these cases as evidence that RSI improves sprint speed. The 160 kg ankle catch must not become a target.

**Example** — Screening question for a strong but non-reactive athlete: "Is this athlete's RSI low relative to his iso push ×BW?" If yes, he fits the sprinter case, and Natera would add ankle switches and catches after an eccentric calf base.

**Related** — [[principle--isometric-overload-for-upright-running]] — the rationale these cases are offered to illustrate.

## Summary

A university football performance staff member uses Catapult data, sliced play by play in OpenField, to compare what offensive linemen do in games with what they do in practice. He argues that total player load looks alike for linemen and wide receivers, but the make-up differs: linemen have contacts, short work bouts and little high-speed running. Practice contact load was far below game level, which he says risked detraining and a spike on Saturday. The talk also covers how he gained coach buy-in, a sprint-speed myth, and a practice-schedule change moving intensity to Friday. The evidence is one team and one season, with no controlled outcome.

## Key claims

- Coaches rely on subjective grading, and objective data reduce opinion-versus-opinion conflict [01:02] [01:32].
- Training should start from game demands and work backwards [02:02].
- A published group study reported what linemen cover in a game, but the speaker argues it reports load, not the actual demands [03:04].
- Linemen and wide receivers have similar total player load, but very different composition (explosive yardage, high-speed distance, max speed) [03:34].
- A line coach ignored his report until the data were reframed in terms the coach cared about [04:04] [04:34].
- A gyroscope-based line metric detects when a lineman drops into a stance, then counts contacts and load per contact [05:38].
- Runs bring more contact and passes bring more force absorption [07:13].
- Practice was far below game intensity in contact load, even on the most intense practice day [08:16] [08:47].
- Energy-system detraining may occur if the alactic system is only stimulated on game day [08:47].
- Even contact periods in practice (first-team offense versus first-team defense, scout team) gave few game-like reps [09:18] [09:48].
- Speed is overrated for football: very few plays reach 90% of max speed [11:21].
- Intensity should rise while volume holds, because raising both creates fatigue [15:35].
- Moving the fast session to Friday (instead of a walkthrough) raised subjective and objective readiness on game day in his program [16:05] [16:36].
- Athletes must be shown their own data to get buy-in, or they feel like "lab rats" [17:38].
- A compromise with receivers: trim low-value periods and ask for full speed in the remaining ones, with load unchanged [18:08].

## Numbers and definitions

- Lineman game distance from the cited study: about 3,600 yards [01:32].
- Player load: summed movement from the unit, described as a more elaborate step counter [03:34].
- Average play duration: about 8 seconds, 7 for a run and 8 for a pass [06:10].
- Time between plays: about 30 seconds for his team, not up-tempo; some teams aim for under 18 seconds [06:42].
- Average load per contact: about 2.12 for pass, 2.32 for run, 2.22 combined [06:42] [07:13] [07:45].
- Contacts per game for a lineman: about 45 [07:13].
- Most intense practice: load per contact 1.54 against 2.22 in games [08:47].
- Alactic stimulus guideline: lose it if not stimulated every five to eight days [08:47].
- Game-like reps in practice: about 3.5 in one period and 1.5 in another, around five total [09:48].
- Contacts as a share of game player load: caption says "a hundred sixty-six percent" and then "sixty six percent", so likely 66% (caption garbled) [10:19].
- Contact load rises by over 100% from practice to game [10:19].
- Work-to-rest ratio about 1 to 3.75 [10:50].
- Fewer than 1% of more than 1,000 plays reached 90% of max speed [11:21].
- Average lineman travel per play: 13.5 yards, with direction split about 25% left and 25% right [11:52].
- Target for skill players: about 75% of game high-speed distance in practice [13:27].
- Three-hour camp practice example: about 7,000 yards for a skill player, pacing at 17 to 18 mph [15:05].
- Eight-second work bouts fall under ten seconds all-out, treated as alactic [10:50].

## Methods and frameworks named

- OpenField used to slice each play in the game files [04:04].
- Offensive-line metric from the gyroscope: stance detection, contacts, load per contact, percent contact load [05:38].
- Practice versus game comparison by period type (individual, seven on seven, team versus scout) [09:18].
- Bioenergetic profile (work, rest) plus a movement profile to define what a lineman needs [12:22].
- Tapered week with a Friday fast session, tracked with wellness questionnaires and heart rate variability from a wearable [16:05].

## Limits and open questions

- One program and one season, no sample size given for contacts or practice periods.
- No evidence that closing the gap changes performance or injury. A question on this was asked and answered with his current approach, not outcomes [14:35] [15:05].
- Adding contact is limited by concussion risk, and the speaker had not yet solved this [12:22] [12:52].
- Heart rate variability is described as mixed: good and bad signals [16:05].
- The "Fast Friday" result is his team's own change, no controls.
- The speaker presents on behalf of Kentucky and the sponsor Catapult, who supply the units, and the caption suggests a company-sponsored session.
- Garbled captions: contacts-share percentage, and some wording in [05:06] and [10:50].

## Q&A

- Evidence that raising practice intensity helps game performance or fatigue: keep load constant and raise intensity, shorter sharper practices, and the Friday change [14:35] [15:05].
- Heart rate variability and wellness use: used, mixed results, Friday intensity improved readiness [16:05] [16:36].
- Player pushback (the Eagles with Chip Kelly were cited as an earlier case): show athletes their data and trim wasted periods so intensity is high in the remaining ones [17:38] [18:08].
- Contact: the speaker invites email and Twitter follow-up [18:38].

## Summary

Two industrial and organizational psychologists describe a one-hour psychological assessment given to every player at the NFL combine since 2013. It measures cognitive ability and personality traits tied to football, and is meant as an addition to physical and film evidence. A three-year validation study compared combine scores with coach ratings of players after at least a year, plus penalties and injuries. Correlations are modest (about 0.22 to 0.35) but the speakers show that top and bottom scorers are rated very differently. The second half describes player-type clusters, a bust-rate comparison using a public value metric, and planned longitudinal modeling of second contracts.

## Key claims

- The goal was to add a standardized psychological measure alongside combine physical tests, not to replace them [04:13], [06:17].
- A league study with team executives produced 16 factors, with intelligence and personality as the two key areas [05:46].
- Intelligence items cover learning, thinking quickly and avoiding mental errors; personality items cover leadership, teamwork, self-control, dependability, preparedness and team fit [06:50].

27	Two industrial and organizational psychologists describe a one-hour psychological assessment given to every player at the NFL combine since 2013.
