A three-year validation study compared combine scores with coach ratings of players after at least a year, plus penalties and injuries. Correlations are modest (about 0.22 to 0.35) but the speakers show that top and bottom scorers are rated very differently. The second half describes player-type clusters, a bust-rate comparison using a public value metric, and planned longitudinal modeling of second contracts.
28	
29	## Key claims
30	
31	- The goal was to add a standardized psychological measure alongside combine physical tests, not to replace them [04:13], [06:17].
32	- A league study with team executives produced 16 factors, with intelligence and personality as the two key areas [05:46].
33	- Intelligence items cover learning, thinking quickly and avoiding mental errors; personality items cover leadership, teamwork, self-control, dependability, preparedness and team fit [06:50].
34	- The test has run at the combine since 2013 with full participation, and the data were also turned into a coaching report [07:20], [07:51].
35	- The validation compared pre-draft scores with coach ratings after the players had been on a team for at least a year [09:54].
36	- The speaker calls correlations of this size good for behavioral science and says they are uncorrected [10:24].
37	- High, middle and low test scores matched coach rating bands; coaches were more straightforward than expected [12:27], [12:59].
38	- Low scorers on intelligence were about three times as likely to be rated poor as star; high scorers about three times as likely rated star [13:30].
39	- Personality: low scorers were about four times as likely to be rated low, high scorers about four and a half times as likely rated high [14:32].
40	- Intelligence and personality together predicted some ratings better, such as decisions under stress [15:33], [16:03].
41	- Decisions under stress also correlated with penalties per play and yards per penalty, and the result held in a larger sample [16:35], [17:07].
42	- Personality variables relate to injuries only weakly, with significance, in an early study; injury type has not been examined [17:37], [18:07].
43	- Cluster analysis found nine player types combining coach-rated physical talent and the psychological scores [22:16].
44	- A "whole package" cluster had a lower bust rate than a low-on-everything cluster, and two clusters with opposite strengths had the same failure rate [24:19], [25:20].
45	- The speakers argue this approach can find undervalued players and de-risk draft and contract decisions [25:51].
46	- Planned work: longitudinal models for second-contract decisions [26:53], [27:24].
47	
48	## Numbers and definitions
49	
50	- Test length: one hour [07:20]. Almost 100 players tested the morning of the talk [28:26].
51	- Validation: three years, 1,500 player scores, about 330 combine participants per year (plus a Super Regional), about 70 percent team participation across all 32 teams [08:52], [09:22].
52	- Coach ratings on about 24 dimensions after at least a year; about 500 players with performance data [09:54].
53	- Coaches' scale of about seven points [12:59].
54	- Correlations (captions read "0 28," "about3," "a0 29," "about 35," "0 22"): about 0.28 [10:24], about 0.3 for the cognitive composite [10:56], about 0.29 for personality [11:26], about 0.35 combined [15:33], 0.22 for decisions under stress [16:03]. The captions garble the decimal points; these are the likeliest readings.
55	- Top and bottom groups each about 25 percent of the sample [12:27].
56	- Rated low by coaches 13 percent of the time, good to great 87 percent (high intelligence scorers) [14:01]; 91 percent good to great (strong personality scorers) [15:02].
57	- Larger penalty sample about 400 players [17:07].
58	- Clusters: nine profiles from 2014 to 2016 data, shown as z-scores [22:16].
59	- "Approximate value" of four or below is read as a bust, about half of drafted players; six or above counts as successful [23:48], [24:19]. Bust rate 41 percent in the "whole package" cluster and 83 percent in the low cluster [24:19]. A "0%" figure for the six-or-above line in the low cluster is stated at [24:50]; the caption is unclear.
60	- Pick 199 in the sixth round (Tom Brady, 2000 draft) as an example of misses [03:11].
61	
62	## Methods and frameworks named
63	
64	- Competency model from a team-executive study; subscale items built from intelligence and personality dimensions [05:46], [06:50].
65	- Criterion validation against coach ratings, penalties, yards per penalty and injuries [09:54], [17:07], [17:37].
66	- Cluster analysis and mixture models for player types [21:46]; Pro Football Reference approximate value as the outcome [23:48].
67	- Planned longitudinal modeling [26:53].
68	
69	## Limits and open questions
70	
71	- The main outcome is coach opinion; the talk does not say whether coaches saw the test results [09:22].
72	- No confidence intervals, sample sizes by cluster or position breakdowns are shown for the clusters [22:16], [25:20].
73	- Injury relationship is small and unreported in effect size [17:37].
74	- Rookie-year and one-to-two-year outcomes only; long-term is future work [26:23].
75	- The speakers sell or run the assessment; Harold Goldstein, a co-author, was absent [00:03].
76	- Several names and terms are mis-captioned ("Wonderlick," "Dbacks," "Yak").

## Summary

The speaker argues that how analysts frame a finding decides whether it is adopted, and tests that idea against four common complaints about the rise of the three-point shot: that the league has become a jump shooting league, that long shots cause long rebounds and fast breaks, that the mid-range game is lost, and that defenses can control three-point percentage. In each case he grants a grain of truth, shows what the data says, and offers a replacement story. He closes with the causes he sees behind the rise in threes and calls his account a theory to be improved. He says his work for the team is private, so the talk avoids team specifics.

## Key claims

- The meta point: statistics have to be tied to a story and a mechanism to be accepted, because fans, coaches and front-office people hold strong prior beliefs [01:30], [02:00], [02:30].
- The goal of framing is to give people permission to accept a new narrative [03:00].
- Ten of the last twelve NBA finalists ranked in the top ten in three-point rate that season [04:00].
- The league has always taken many jump shots: the share of shots from beyond ten feet was the same in 1999-2000 and last year, so the change is in distance, not in jump shooting [04:32].
- Taking more long jump shots can be described as settling or as using the geometry of the court, and the description changes how it is heard [06:03].
- Long misses do produce longer rebounds, but they do not produce more fast breaks than other misses [06:35].
- Shots rebounded from around the rim lead to fast breaks more often than rebounded above-the-break threes [07:07].
- His explanation is that a three usually follows good execution and balanced spacing, so a defender is already back; this is his own account [08:10].
- The mid-range share has fallen, but the self-created (unassisted) mid-range shots by star players have held roughly steady [08:43], [09:44].
- Among high-usage players, long two-pointers rose as a share of made shots over about fifteen years [10:44].
- Unassisted above-the-break threes by star players have risen sharply in four years, driven by a small number of players [11:16], [11:47].
- Baseball analogies hold for rate stats and efficiency, but basketball has no batting order, and a possession has a third outcome besides made or missed: not shooting [13:18], [13:48], [14:18].
- A well-contested shot often means the player did not shoot at all [15:18].
- Defensive three-point percentage looks like a coin flip at the individual level, and the speaker says it is not necessarily luck [16:18], [16:48].
- Defenders can affect a shot in known ways: distance to the shooter, avoiding fouls on a jump shooter, and late-clock or end-game contests [16:48], [17:18], [17:48].
- Defending the three therefore means avoiding it, since a three-point shot at lower than a certain accuracy is not taken [18:19].
- Four factors behind more threes: player skill development, teams permitting players to shoot from farther, downsizing, and strategies that move where the ball is caught [18:50], [19:20], [19:50].
- Power forwards' three-point rates have risen in four years and teams more often play four or five shooters [20:20].
- He calls all this a theory and invites better ones, aiming to be "less wrong" [21:22].

## Numbers and definitions

- Jump shot (his definition): a shot from outside ten feet. Share was 55% in 1999-2000 and 55% last year [04:32].
- Shots from outside fifteen feet: began at 42%, peaked at 48%, about 46% now [04:32], [05:02].
- Mid-range (his definition): outside the paint, inside the three-point arc [08:43].
- High-usage player (his definition, "arbitrary"): usage of 27% or higher [10:44].
- Share of made shots that are long twos for that group: from 7% to 11.5%, which he calls over a 50% increase, over fifteen years [10:44].
- Extra unassisted threes last year versus the 2000 rate: about 340, of which two players accounted for 308 [11:47]. He said he may have done the math wrong.

# 17 km/h ≈ 55-60% MV, 27 km/h ≈ 85% MV, For This AFL Cohort

**What it is** — Harries states the organization's fixed GPS speed-zone cutoffs converted, for these athletes, to roughly: high-speed running threshold (17 km/h) ≈ 55-60% of max velocity; sprint threshold (27 km/h) ≈ 85% of max velocity "for most of our athletes in that club" (~09:57-10:17, ~22:54-23:11). Very-high-speed running (23 km/h) sits between the two; the entry writer's calculation from his own two figures puts it at roughly 72-80% MV, though Harries does not state that conversion explicitly.

**Why it works** — This is a cohort-average conversion, presented as an observed fact about this specific group of AFL athletes' typical max velocities relative to the club's fixed absolute speed zones, not a derived or universal formula.

**When to apply** — Use as a worked example of *how* to convert an absolute GPS speed threshold into a %MV figure for a given population, and as the reason a fixed km/h threshold behaves differently across athletes with different MVs (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]).

**When NOT to apply** — This conversion is specific to Harries' AFL cohort's own average max velocities; it should not be applied to Baylor football athletes, whose MV distribution (and therefore the %MV a given km/h threshold represents) will differ by sport and very likely by position. Baylor's own speed-zone thresholds are not yet position-specific (`method-baseline.md`), so the correct move is to compute the equivalent conversion from Baylor's own Catapult MV data per player or position group, not to reuse these percentages.

**Example** — A Baylor GPS threshold set generically at, say, 16 km/h for "high-speed running" would represent a very different %MV for a 30 km/h-MV wide receiver than for a 24 km/h-MV offensive lineman; this claim is the reminder to check that conversion per player/position rather than assume it.

# The Pre-Competitive Microcycle: Cut Volume Hard, Raise Maximal-Speed and Sport-Specific Work, Keep Frequency

**What it is** — The pre-competitive microcycle forms the content of the realization
mesocycle (see [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]]), and it is the
realization mesocycle itself, not this microcycle, that the book calls "traditionally...
termed the taper" (PDF p. 122, printed p. 111) (PDF pp. 104-105, printed pp. 93-94; verified
against page images, re-checked 2026-09-27). It must satisfy three demands (PDF p. 104, printed p. 93): sport-specific
exercises/tasks that simulate the forthcoming competition and build mental readiness and
toughness; development of maximal speed/power and sport-specific quickness; and full (or
partial) restoration after the preceding transmutation mesocycle's fatiguing workloads. Table

# Define a Lineman's Game Demand by Slicing Each Play and Counting Contacts, Then Train Backwards From It

**What it is** — Chris Morris (University of Kentucky, introduced as the speaker for the sponsor Catapult) describes a method for working out what a position actually does in a game. Step 1: "we train for the demands of the game" and "work our way backwards" (QLdbKUiNadg [02:02]). Step 2: a published group study of linemen reported about 3,600 yards of game distance, but Morris says that figure is load, not the demands of the game (QLdbKUiNadg [01:32], [03:04]). Step 3: upload every game file to OpenField (Catapult's analytics platform) and "slice each individual play" (QLdbKUiNadg [04:04]). Step 4: use Catapult's offensive-line metric. A gyroscope in the unit recognizes when the lineman drops into his stance, which marks a play start, then the software counts contacts, load per contact and percent of load that is contact (QLdbKUiNadg [05:38]). Step 5: add a bioenergetic profile (work time, rest time) and a movement profile (distance and direction per play). From his own season: average play about 8 seconds (7 for a run, 8 for a pass), about 30 seconds between plays for his non-up-tempo offense, about 45 contacts per game, load per contact about 2.12 on passes, 2.32 on runs, 2.22 combined (QLdbKUiNadg [06:10], [06:42], [07:13], [07:45]). Work-to-rest was about 1 to 3.75 (QLdbKUiNadg [10:50], [11:21]), and an average play covered 13.5 yards, split about 25% left and 25% right (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). The caption spelling of the position metric is "offensive la Mettrie" (QLdbKUiNadg [05:38]), and the passage on what the gyroscope captures "the next five seconds" is garbled (QLdbKUiNadg [06:10]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's stated reason is that total load hides what makes up the load, so the composition has to be measured before practice can be designed (QLdbKUiNadg [03:34], [04:04]). The speaker gives no mechanism for why contact-per-play counts predict injury or performance, and none is claimed. Inference: the value is descriptive. Once a position has a profile (contacts, load per contact, work:rest, yards per play), any practice period can be scored against it.

**When to apply** — When a coach or staff member asks "what does this position need?" and the only available answer is a distance or total-load number. Eric's baseline: "No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist" in a formal sense, and Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q7): "They do not exist formally." Inference: this method is one way to build a position-level profile from Baylor's own Catapult game files, since Baylor already runs Catapult and OpenField.

**When NOT to apply** — One program, one season, one position group (offensive line), with no sample size given for plays or games (QLdbKUiNadg [06:10] to [07:45]). The stance-detection metric depends on Catapult hardware and software that the speaker presents on behalf of the vendor, so it is not a vendor-neutral result. The speaker does not show that matching the profile in practice changes performance or injury. The averages (8 seconds, 30 seconds, 45 contacts) belong to Kentucky's offense in his season; an up-tempo offense will differ, as he says himself (QLdbKUiNadg [06:42], [11:21]). Do not import Kentucky's numbers as Baylor targets.

**Example** — From the talk: the average lineman play lasts about 8 seconds and costs a load per contact near 2.22, so the energy-system and contact demand is repeated sub-10-second efforts, and a practice period is judged by how close it gets to that (QLdbKUiNadg [07:45], [10:50]).

**Related** — [[claim--lineman-practice-contact-load-well-below-game]], [[claim--equal-player-load-different-composition-line-vs-receivers]], [[claim--fewer-than-one-percent-of-plays-reach-90-percent-max-speed]]; existing library: [[principle--percent-of-game-value-as-volume-metric]] (Harries, running volume as percent of game value), [[claim--speed-threshold-percent-of-max-velocity-conversion]] (Harries, threshold conversion by cohort).

# Kentucky's Linemen Practiced at About Two-Thirds of Game Load per Contact, With About Five Game-Like Reps

**What it is** — Morris compared practice to game using the line metric. His reported figures:
- Average game load per contact 2.22; on the most intense practice day (Tuesday) 1.54 (QLdbKUiNadg [08:16], [08:47]).
- The practice week was supposed to peak on Tuesday, and distance was fine, but contact and load per contact were not (QLdbKUiNadg [08:16], [08:47]).
- Only first-team offense against first-team defense, and one-on-ones, came near game intensity; team versus scout team gave the most contact load, but scout players "don't go nearly as hard" (QLdbKUiNadg [09:18], [09:48]).
- About 3.5 game-like reps in one period and 1.5 in another, "about five game reps in a practice" (QLdbKUiNadg [09:48]).
- In games, contacts account for about 66% of total player load (the caption says "a hundred sixty-six percent" and then "sixty six percent", read here as 66%, QLdbKUiNadg [10:19]).
- "By the time we get to the game we increase our contact load by over a hundred percent" (QLdbKUiNadg [10:19]).
The line coach "was astounded" because he believed the sessions were good (QLdbKUiNadg [09:48]). Morris says the line had a problem he had not solved: adding contact raises concussion risk (QLdbKUiNadg [12:22], [12:52]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation for the gap is social: scout players hold back out of an unspoken bond with first-team players (QLdbKUiNadg [09:48]). He also argues there is a mental component, that low-intensity practice "doesn't resonate" in games (QLdbKUiNadg [12:52]); he gives no evidence for that. Inference: measuring load per contact exposes a gap that total player load, which looked fine on Tuesday, hid.

**When to apply** — When practice is believed to be "hard" because athletes say so. Compare a metric that measures the demand (here load per contact) with the game value, period by period. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Inference: the coach's own question here ("how much are they banging in practice?", QLdbKUiNadg [07:13]) is the kind of question that passes that rule.

**When NOT to apply** — One team and one season; no sample sizes for periods, games or athletes; no spread values. No outcome is shown: the talk does not report that closing the gap changed performance or injuries (the audience question asked this and the answer described the current approach, QLdbKUiNadg [14:35], [15:05]). The metric is vendor specific (Catapult), and the 2.22 benchmark is Kentucky's. The practical problem he names, concussion risk, limits how much contact to add, and his proposed substitute (stance, fire off, hit a dummy, swim move, accelerate five yards) was only being considered, not tested (QLdbKUiNadg [12:52]). At Baylor, contact exposure is also an Athletic Medicine concern; Inference: any added contact needs their input.

**Example** — From the talk: 1.54 on the hardest Tuesday against 2.22 in games (QLdbKUiNadg [08:47]).

# If the Alactic System Is Stimulated Only on Saturday, It May Detrain: A Five-to-Eight-Day Rule of Thumb

**What it is** — Morris says that "from a physiologist standpoint" an energy system responsible for alactic power is lost if it is not stimulated "every five to eight days", so a lineman who only does game-like work on Saturday "was potentially detraining across the season" (QLdbKUiNadg [08:47]). He classifies the lineman's work as alactic: efforts of about 8 seconds, "anything less than ten all-out", repeated, with a work-to-rest ratio of about 1 to 3.75 (QLdbKUiNadg [10:50], [11:21]). The assertion is stated as a general fact with no citation.

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and no source for the five-to-eight-day figure. Inference: it is a detraining (loss of a trained quality without re-exposure) argument, and it sits in the same range as Issurin's residual duration for maximum speed (alactic), 5 ± 3 days, in the existing library entry below. Issurin's table is about a different population and different quality (maximal speed), so this is a similarity, not a confirmation.

**When to apply** — As a planning prompt: check when, in the week, each position group gets its most game-like, brief, all-out exposure. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16): "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q15) describes the in-season game week as heavy lift Monday, heavy practice Tuesday and Wednesday, and lifting and hard practice ending 72 hours before a Saturday game.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: an assertion with no data shown. The talk measures contact load in practice versus game but never measures loss of alactic capacity, so "potentially detraining" is a hypothesis about Kentucky's linemen. Do not read the range as an Issurin-style tested figure for line play. It applies to a quality (repeated alactic power efforts) that the speaker says matches an 8-second play, and it should not be extended to other energy systems.

**Example** — Inference: a line group that has a speed or short-effort exposure Tuesday and Wednesday but only walkthroughs after that goes about 72 hours with no all-out work before a Saturday game; that is the pattern the speaker worries about (QLdbKUiNadg [16:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--lineman-practice-contact-load-well-below-game]], [[case-study--fast-friday-flip-from-friday-walkthrough]]; existing library: [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] (Issurin), [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] (Issurin).

# In Over 1,000 Plays From One Season, Fewer Than 1% Reached 90% of a Player's Max Speed

**What it is** — Morris reports that of "over the thousand plays" he broke down from the previous season, "less than 1%" at "any position" reached 90% of that player's max velocity (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). On an average lineman play, travel was 13.5 yards, with direction about 25% left and 25% right (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). His conclusion: football is "a game of acceleration" more than of top speed, because a player seldom gets 20 to 30 yards without contact or a change of direction (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). He says this was "shocking" to the head coach and the strength coach, "all about speed" (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). The slide's position breakdown is not captioned, and "the big" is the group he specifies for the 13.5-yard figure ("for our big specifically", QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]).

**Why it works** — Stated by the speaker: short distances, contact and direction changes cut off the chance to build speed (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). Nothing beyond that is given. Inference: because the metric is a percent of each player's own max, a fast player's 90% is a higher absolute speed than a slow player's, so this is a statement about exposure to near-max effort per player, not about absolute mph.

**When to apply** — When deciding how much of a position's practice or conditioning should be spent at near-max velocity versus accelerating and decelerating. Check it against Baylor's own game files per position group before acting. Eric's baseline: "No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist" formally (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q7: "They do not exist formally."). Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16) states that Issurin's residual effects, in which speed fades fastest, drive speed programming. Inference: Morris's count is about game exposure to near-max speed, whereas the Issurin point is about how long a trained quality persists; they answer different questions and the combination is not tested in this talk.

**When NOT to apply** — One program and one season; the number of plays is only "over a thousand", position and level of play (Kentucky's college offense) are not broken down in the audio. It does not show that max-speed training is unimportant: it shows a low frequency of 90% exposures in games. A player who does reach 90% in a play may still decide that play. The captions run together "90% of their max" with an unclear phrase ("max B"), so treat the exact metric as caption-garbled (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). Existing library entries on the Harries AFL cohort set the max-velocity decision gates at 75-85% and above 90%, so the cut point here is a convention, not a threshold with evidence.

**Example** — From the talk: the strength coach built around speed, while the 1,000-play breakdown showed almost no play at 90% of max (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]).

# Case Study: Moving the Fast Session From Thursday to Friday at Kentucky

**What it is** — Morris describes one program's in-season change (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05], [16:36]).
- **Before:** Monday to Wednesday practice, Thursday the faster practice, Friday a complete walkthrough, Saturday game. With an evening Saturday game that left "48 hours potentially 72 hours" with little central-nervous-system or bioenergetic stimulus, and athletes "ended up coming out flat" (QLdbKUiNadg [16:36]).
- **Change:** a "fast Friday", keeping intensity on Friday while volume stays low.
- **Reported effect:** "our readiness will go you know through the roof both subjectively and objectively on game day"; the heart rate variability device ("mega wave", caption spelling) had shifted more parasympathetic under the old pattern, and subjective wellness rose on Saturday after the flip (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05], [16:36], [17:07]).
- **Measures:** wellness questionnaires plus a heart rate variability wearable, with the explicit caveat that heart rate variability gives "good things and bad things" (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05]).
- **Linemen detail:** linemen "don't do anything on Fridays" and the Friday drop is their lowest day, so they need the stimulation as much as the skill players (QLdbKUiNadg [13:58]). Skill players target about 75% of game high-speed distance in the week (QLdbKUiNadg [13:27]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that a long gap with no stimulation leaves the nervous system and energy systems flat for the game (QLdbKUiNadg [16:36]). He gives no data or test of that mechanism. Inference: it could also be that the athletes simply feel better with a familiar-intensity day, which the talk cannot separate.

**When to apply** — As an option to examine for evening or late-kickoff games where hard work ends three days out. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q15) describes Baylor's game week as Sunday off, Monday heavy lift, Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice with a lighter lift Wednesday, and "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game". Inference: the rule of ending hard work 72 hours out and the Fast Friday pattern are different designs, and this talk cannot decide between them. Eric's baseline: Eric's own SportSmith writing states that subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes learned to game them (`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`), so the subjective half of this evidence is the half he has distrusted.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one team's own change, no control, no numbers shown for the readiness changes, and no result on performance or injury. The speaker reports mixed value of heart rate variability. Wellness scores are subjective. Do not cite as evidence that Friday intensity improves game performance. Do not copy it into a Baylor week without Athletic Performance and the head coach, because it conflicts with the 72-hour rule above.

**Example** — The talk's own sequence: Thursday fast day plus Friday walkthrough replaced by Friday fast day, then readiness read from wellness and heart rate variability on Saturday (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05], [16:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--alactic-detraining-if-stimulated-only-on-game-day]], [[heuristic--hold-volume-raise-intensity-trim-low-value-periods]]; existing library: [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] and [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] (Issurin; the same logic of cutting volume while keeping maximal-speed and specific work before competition).

# Hold Total Load, Raise Intensity: Trim Low-Value Practice Periods and Ask for Full Speed in the Rest

**What it is** — Asked whether there is evidence that raising practice workload changes game performance or fatigue, Morris answered with his approach, not evidence (QLdbKUiNadg [14:35], [15:05]):
- "maintain load", control load, "increase our intensity", and prefer shorter, more intense practices (QLdbKUiNadg [15:05]).
- "You can't increase the intensity and volume" together "because then you create massive amounts of fatigue"; wellness questionnaires help judge internal load next to external load (QLdbKUiNadg [15:35]).
- Camp example: in a three-hour practice a skill player may cover about 7,000 yards but "he's just gonna pace", at "1718 miles an hour" (caption; read as 17 to 18 mph in the summary). The quarterback's timing is then off when receivers move faster in a game (QLdbKUiNadg [15:05], [15:35]).
- With wide receivers, the compromise was to pull back seven-on-seven blitz-package periods where they were "just running routes for no reason", so they run full speed in the remaining seven-on-seven and team periods, with load unchanged (QLdbKUiNadg [18:08]).
- Target for skill players: about 75% of game high-speed distance during the week (QLdbKUiNadg [13:27]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is that athletes pace themselves when practice is long, so the pace they learn is not the pace of the game (QLdbKUiNadg [15:05]). The claim that both volume and intensity cannot rise without fatigue is stated as fact without evidence (QLdbKUiNadg [15:35]). Inference: this is a restatement of constant-load, higher-intensity redistribution and relies on external load (GPS) staying equal while the mix changes.

**When to apply** — In camp or in-season when practices run long and speed is low per period. Eric's baseline: Eric's playbook states the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21`), tagged Inferred (course-team position, individual speaker unconfirmed). Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q18): "I don't have the specific sets and reps." Inference: Morris's version adds the practical lever (cut low-value periods, name the intensity expected in the rest).

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker's assertion and one camp example. He says plainly he had not studied the interventions closely enough to answer with evidence (QLdbKUiNadg [14:35]). The 17 to 18 mph figure is a caption problem and implausible as a sustained pace; do not quote it. The "75% of game high-speed distance" target is Kentucky's for skill players, not a validated number. Athlete and coach consent matters, as the speaker's own Eagles anecdote shows (see the related entry).

**Example** — The wide-receiver compromise above: fewer seven-on-seven blitz-pack reps, full speed in the ones that remain, unchanged load (QLdbKUiNadg [18:08]).

**Related** — [[claim--lineman-practice-contact-load-well-below-game]], [[case-study--fast-friday-flip-from-friday-walkthrough]], [[heuristic--show-coaches-and-athletes-the-data-in-their-terms]]; existing library: [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] (Issurin).

# If a Coach Ignores the Report, Change the Question, Then Show Athletes Their Own Data

**What it is** — Three episodes from Morris's talk:
- **The trashed report.** He put a report he was "really proud of" on the offensive-line coach's desk and the coach threw it in the trash (QLdbKUiNadg [04:04]). His first reaction was that he had a PhD and was the expert; he then concluded that his data "was not having the right conversation" (QLdbKUiNadg [04:34]).
- **The reframe.** The coach later asked "how much they're bangin in practice" (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13]). Morris answered by first measuring the game (about 45 contacts, load per contact about 2.22) so the practice figures were comparable (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13], [07:45]).
- **Athlete buy-in.** Athletes must be "connected" to their data internally and externally, "because if you don't they don't have a lot of buy-in they feel like lab rats" (QLdbKUiNadg [17:38]). He mentions an earlier case, the Eagles under Chip Kelly, where players pushed back on more intense work (QLdbKUiNadg [17:38]).
He also notes that coaches grade in subjective terms, and without objective data a dispute is "just your opinion versus my opinion" (QLdbKUiNadg [01:02], [01:32]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that the report answered a question the coach was not asking. He gives no evidence beyond his own experience. Inference: a coach's own question (here, contact in practice versus game) gets attention, while a generic report does not.

**When to apply** — When a coach does not read or use a report. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." Inference: the coach's question is the "where to look", and the data answer it. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): "Strength staff will build it most likely; we don't have sport science support for most teams." Inference: at Baylor the person who reframes the report for the coach is often the strength staff member.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: anecdote, a single coach, a single athlete group. The talk does not report whether the reframed reports changed decisions or results. It does not support using data to win arguments with a coach; the speaker describes the reverse (first reaction: "you should listen to me", QLdbKUiNadg [04:34]). The Eagles reference is a second-hand recollection by the speaker.

**Example** — The talk's own: the practice-versus-game contact comparison was built because the line coach wanted to see "how much they're bangin" (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13]).

**Related** — [[claim--lineman-practice-contact-load-well-below-game]], [[heuristic--hold-volume-raise-intensity-trim-low-value-periods]], [[framework--frame-findings-with-story-mechanism-and-grain-of-truth]]; existing library: [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] (Old Bull).

# Validate an Assessment Before Using It: Score Early, Rate Later, Correlate

**What it is** — The first speaker (caption spelling "Ken yuso"; he thanks co-authors "Charles sheram" and Harold Goldstein, 40NV3_u9tYY [00:03]) describes a three-step validation of the NFL's one-hour psychological test. His background: industrial and organizational psychologists, "heavy litigation, employment discrimination" work, where "you have to demonstrate that what you're measuring actually is connected to some meaningful outcome" (40NV3_u9tYY [08:21], [08:52]). Design as reported:

# Top and Bottom Test-Score Quartiles Were Rated Three to Four and a Half Times Apart by Coaches

**What it is** — To make correlations of about 0.3 usable, the first speaker (caption spelling "Ken yuso") splits scores into high, medium and low; high and low each hold "about 25% of the sample", and the coaches' ratings (a scale of about seven points) fall into matching bands (40NV3_u9tYY [12:27], [12:59]). Reported results:
- **Intelligence:** low scorers were about three times more likely to be rated "poor performers or disappointments" than stars; high scorers about three times more likely to be rated stars than disappointments (40NV3_u9tYY [13:30]).
- **High intelligence scorers:** rated low by coaches 13% of the time, good to great 87% of the time (40NV3_u9tYY [14:01]).
- **Personality:** low scorers about four times as likely to be rated low as high; high scorers rated high about four and a half times as often; 91% of strong personality scorers rated good to great (40NV3_u9tYY [14:32], [15:02]).
- False positives and false negatives, "the misses", were "pretty low" for the top and bottom groups; the speaker says he is not showing the middle group (40NV3_u9tYY [14:01], [15:02]).
He notes he was "surprised that the coaches were pretty straightforward" in how they used the scale (40NV3_u9tYY [12:59]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond presenting the bands as a way to show what a correlation of this size looks like in a cut-score decision (40NV3_u9tYY [12:27], [14:01]). Inference: with about 0.3 correlation, tails separate more clearly than the middle, so band odds look stronger than the correlation alone suggests.

**When to apply** — When explaining a modest correlation to a coach or director. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." Inference: reporting "top quarter versus bottom quarter" odds is the kind of statement a coach can use to decide where to look.

**When NOT to apply** — The speaker states the middle half, where most decisions fall, was not shown. These odds are for a combine test and coach ratings, in the NFL, for players with at least a year of data; they are not injury or performance results. The bands compare the extremes, and 87% "good to great" is of those rated, with 70% team participation (40NV3_u9tYY [09:22]). No intervals or sample sizes for each band are given. Do not apply as a cut score for athletes: the speaker says the test is meant as an incremental data point (40NV3_u9tYY [06:17]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a high personality score met a "good to great" rating 91% of the time (40NV3_u9tYY [15:02]).

**Related** — [[framework--criterion-validation-of-a-psychological-test-against-coach-ratings]], [[principle--add-standardized-psychological-data-as-increment-not-substitute]].

# Combining Ability and Stress Tolerance Predicted Coach-Rated Decisions Under Stress, and Related to Penalties

**What it is** — The first speaker (caption spelling "Ken yuso") reports that intelligence and personality combined predict some coach ratings better than either alone (overall about 0.35, 40NV3_u9tYY [15:33]). The example is decision-making under stress: combining the intelligence score with the personality stress-tolerance variable gave "a 0.22 correlation" (caption "a0 22") with the coaches' rating of decisions under stress (40NV3_u9tYY [16:03]). His reasoning: a calm player who decides badly does not help, so the interesting question is whether a player continues to decide well under stress (40NV3_u9tYY [16:03], [16:35]). Moving to on-field metrics, this variable "actually correlating with penalties" per play and yards per penalty, standardized across position, with better results for defensive backs ("Dbacks", caption) than across all positions (40NV3_u9tYY [16:35], [17:07]). A larger second sample of about 400 players held the result (40NV3_u9tYY [17:07]). The size of the penalty correlations is not stated aloud ("a pretty nice correlation").

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that decisions under stress need both the cognitive ability to decide well and the personality trait to stay composed (40NV3_u9tYY [16:03], [16:35]). No further mechanism is given. Inference: the combination result is an interaction or additive effect, and the talk does not say which.

**When to apply** — As a model for a measurement design: define the behavior of interest (decide well under pressure), then see which measured traits jointly predict it. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Inference: for Baylor, a question like "who stays accurate when fatigued or loaded" would have to be defined first, with its own criterion.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: 0.22 is the only value given, the penalty correlations have no stated size, and no intervals or position-level results are shown. Penalties are influenced by position, scheme and officiating, which the speaker's "standardize across position" does not remove. The outcome in the main result is coach opinion of decisions, not measured decisions. The finding is for NFL rookies and early-career players on one test, not a general rule for college athletes or for Baylor.

**Example** — The talk's: a calm, cool player who makes lousy decisions versus one who keeps deciding well under stress, with the second the target (40NV3_u9tYY [16:35]).

**Related** — [[framework--criterion-validation-of-a-psychological-test-against-coach-ratings]], [[claim--personality-scores-relate-weakly-to-injury]].

# The "Whole Package" Cluster Busted at 41%, the Low Cluster at 83%, and Opposite-Strength Clusters Failed Equally

**What it is** — The second speaker (caption spelling "Charles sheram") uses Pro Football Reference's "approximate value" (AV) as the outcome. A score of four or below is read as a bust, about half of drafted players; six or above is generally successful (40NV3_u9tYY [23:48], [24:19]). Reported:
- Cluster 7, "the whole package": 41% busts, so "60%" successful (40NV3_u9tYY [24:19]).
- Cluster 6, "low on everything": about 83% unsuccessful (40NV3_u9tYY [24:19]). The speaker also says "0%" of this group reached the six-or-above line (40NV3_u9tYY [24:50]); the caption is unclear.
- Cluster 3 (physical, not psychological) against cluster 9 (psychological, less physical): "the failure rate" is "the same" (40NV3_u9tYY [25:20]).
His reading: a high-risk group and a low-risk group can be told apart, and a team can find undervalued players who are "smart", "dependable" and prepared but not the biggest stars, who "succeed in the NFL roughly at the same rates" as first-round stars (40NV3_u9tYY [25:51]). He compares this to Moneyball (40NV3_u9tYY [25:20]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond the cluster definitions. Inference: AV rewards playing time and production, which depend on both talent and staying on the roster, so character-related traits plausibly matter, but the talk does not test this.

**When to apply** — As an example of testing whether a profile separates outcomes on an independent public metric. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Inference: an equivalent for Baylor would need a defined outcome (for example, games played or availability) and an agreed meaning of "bust".

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: a model result with no validation shown, no cluster sizes, no intervals, and no check that the clusters were not tuned to this outcome. The speaker acknowledges that most of the work covers only a rookie year or one to two years (40NV3_u9tYY [26:23]). AV is a skewed, production-based number that credits playing time, so "bust" is partly a function of roster and scheme. The claim that a low-physical, high-psychological player succeeds at first-round-star rates compares failure rates, not careers. Do not use as a recruiting rule: it is an NFL draft result, and the speaker has a commercial interest in the test.

**Example** — The talk's own: cluster 9 versus cluster 3, opposite makeups with the same failure rate, as the case for finding undervalued players (40NV3_u9tYY [25:20], [25:51]).

**Related** — [[framework--player-type-clusters-from-physical-and-psychological-scores]], [[principle--add-standardized-psychological-data-as-increment-not-substitute]].

# Add a Standardized Psychological Measure as an Increment to Physical Evidence, Not a Replacement

**What it is** — The speakers frame the test as league-wide, standardized data to sit beside the physical combine and pro-day data. The first speaker (caption spelling "Ken yuso") says the existing model leaned on past performance, film and interviews, with psychological variables "not standardized" (40NV3_u9tYY [02:40], [04:13]). The addition: a standardized psychological assessment, one hour, given since 2013 to all combine players (40NV3_u9tYY [07:20]). He is explicit that "these aren't the primary drivers", that the sport is "so dominated by physical attributes", so the measure is "an incremental extra... not a substitute" (40NV3_u9tYY [06:17]). The data were also turned into a coaching report for development: for example, a confident player who decides badly is handled differently from a hesitant player who decides well (40NV3_u9tYY [07:51], [08:21]). The second speaker (caption spelling "Charles sheram") ends: the psychological piece is what is missing "on a systematic league wide level", "standardized" and "efficient" (40NV3_u9tYY [27:55], [28:26]). He contrasts a Tom Brady pick (199th, 2000 draft) as an example of misses (40NV3_u9tYY [03:11]).

**Why it works** — The speakers' stated reason: returns from more metrics on the same data are "shrinking", so new data that are standardized and cheap to collect add information (40NV3_u9tYY [03:41]). The speaker credits a panel remark for the "shrinking returns" point and gives no data for it. Inference: adding a different kind of measure is more likely to add information than a finer version of an existing measure.

**When to apply** — When a decision rests on informal, non-standardized information (interviews, impressions). Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." Inference: a standardized psychological measure belongs in the same sequence, as something to direct attention, not to decide alone.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is the speakers' framing, supported only by modest correlations and the clusters in the related entries. The speakers run or sell the assessment, and Harold Goldstein, a co-author, was absent (40NV3_u9tYY [00:03]). The longitudinal part, who ramps up or fades after a second contract, was planned work, not a result (40NV3_u9tYY [26:53], [27:24]). Psychological testing of athletes raises consent and data-governance questions that the talk does not address; Inference: at Baylor, that would need review before collection.

**Example** — The talk's own: almost 100 players tested in one hour on the morning of the talk (40NV3_u9tYY [28:26]).

**Related** — [[framework--criterion-validation-of-a-psychological-test-against-coach-ratings]], [[claim--score-bands-map-to-coach-rating-odds]], [[claim--whole-package-cluster-has-lower-bust-rate]]; existing library: [[farrell-2024-beyond-the-box-score-using-psychological-metrics-to-forecast-nba-success]] (research brief on psychological metrics and NBA success).

# To Change a Prior Belief, Grant the Grain of Truth, Show the Data, and Replace the Story

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now"; director of basketball research for the Milwaukee Bucks, as he states at BJkCqf6Fj2w [00:30]) says the "meta point" of his talk is that "the way we talk about our statistical insights is a vital thing towards them actually being adopted" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [01:30]). His reasoning:
- Citing Kahneman and Tversky (caption spelling "conman tki"), he says the human mind is "really bad" at statistical information not attached to a narrative or a mechanism (BJkCqf6Fj2w [02:00]).
- People in sport have "very strong prior opinions", often based in fact; "it's not just enough to say well here's some stats that tell you you're wrong" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [02:30]).
- The aim is to give people "the permission" to accept a new narrative (BJkCqf6Fj2w [03:00]).
- His procedure, applied to four complaints about the three-point shot: state the belief, grant its "grain of truth" (many such narratives are "completely true" in part), show what the data say, then offer a better explanation of why (BJkCqf6Fj2w [03:30], [08:10]). For example, the same fact can be heard as teams "settling" for long jumpers or as using "the geometry of the court" because three is greater than two (BJkCqf6Fj2w [06:03]).
He ends by calling his account a theory and welcoming "better theories", with the goal to be "less wrong" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [21:22]).

**Why it works** — Given by the speaker: a mechanism lets listeners replace the old picture, whereas numbers alone do not (BJkCqf6Fj2w [02:00], [02:30]). He supplies no test showing that framing changes adoption. Inference: this is a claim about communication practice from his experience, not a measured effect.

**When to apply** — When a coach holds a strong belief the data contradict. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." Inference: granting the coach's grain of truth fits that stance, because the eye is treated as a valid pointer. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): "Strength staff will build it most likely; we don't have sport science support for most teams." Inference: strength staff who write coach-facing reports can use the same sequence (belief, grain of truth, data, replacement mechanism).

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker's assertion from his experience and a literature reference, with no evidence of adoption results. His own caution is that the mechanisms in the talk are theory (BJkCqf6Fj2w [21:22]), and a story can persuade without being right: the fast-break explanation below is his hypothesis, not tested (BJkCqf6Fj2w [08:10]). Do not use a reframe to hide a weak finding; the order is data first, then the explanation. It also does not replace working with a coach who has already decided.

**Example** — From the talk: "the NBA has become a jump shooting league" is answered by granting that teams take many jump shots, then showing the share beyond 10 feet was 55% in 1999 to 2000 and 55% the previous season (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:32]).

**Related** — [[claim--jump-shot-share-flat-since-1999-2000-distance-changed]], [[claim--long-rebounds-do-not-produce-more-fast-breaks]]; from this batch (football): [[heuristic--show-coaches-and-athletes-the-data-in-their-terms]]; existing library: [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] (Old Bull).

# The Share of Jump Shots Was 55% in 1999-2000 and 55% Last Year: What Changed Is Distance

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") tests the complaint that "the NBA has become a jump shooting league" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:00]). Reported data, using shot-location data he calls reliable from about 1999-2000:
- Jump shot defined as a shot from outside 10 feet: 55% of shots in 1999-2000 and 55% the previous season (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:32]).
- Using 15 feet: it started near 42%, peaked at 48%, and is "around 46% now" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:32], [05:02]).
- Ten of the last twelve NBA finalists ranked in the top ten in three-point rate that season (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:00]).

**When to apply** — As a worked example of checking a claim about "more of X" against a time series with a fixed definition. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Inference: the transferable move is to fix a definition (here "outside 10 feet") and compare the same measure across years before accepting a trend story, as for any Baylor load metric whose definition or threshold changed.

**When NOT to apply** — Supported, not proven: the numbers were spoken from slides the captions do not describe, and the share outside 15 feet is given as three rounded values. The data are NBA, 1999-2000 to 2016-17. The definition (10 feet) is the speaker's, and he notes a 15-foot choice changes the series. It shows the share of jump shots did not rise; it says nothing about their efficiency. It is not evidence on any other sport or on college basketball.

**Example** — The speaker's own: 55% in 1999-2000 and 55% last year for shots beyond 10 feet (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:32]).

# Long Shots Cause Long Rebounds, but Not More Fast Breaks: Rim-Area Misses Lead to Fast Breaks 1.5 to 2 Times as Often

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") tests the claim that "long shots lead to long rebounds and allow fast breaks" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [06:35]). Part true: a longer shot comes off the rim harder, so the rebound is longer (BJkCqf6Fj2w [06:35]). Part not: using 15 to 20 years of data, a shot from around the rim that is rebounded "is between one and a half and two times more likely to lead to a fast break than an above the break three"; a corner three is "slightly more fast breakable" but much less so than a missed shot in the paint (BJkCqf6Fj2w [07:07]). His account of why we remember it wrongly: the vivid case (a defender closes out, the shooter misses, the defender sprints for a layup) sticks in memory (BJkCqf6Fj2w [07:39]). His explanation of the real pattern: a three usually follows "good execution, good spacing", the floor is balanced, "there's always someone back on defense", and an above-the-break shooter is "already halfway back" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [07:39], [08:10]).

**Why it works** — The data finding (the 1.5 to 2 times comparison) is the speaker's reported result. The explanation about balanced spacing is his own hypothesis: he introduces it with "what I think is happening" and the talk does not test it (BJkCqf6Fj2w [07:39], [08:10]).

**When to apply** — As an example of separating an observed rate from a mechanism story. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Inference: a coach's in-game belief ("that always happens") can be checked against stored game data before changing a plan, if the data are available.

**When NOT to apply** — Supported for the rate comparison, untested for the mechanism. The speaker gives no sample sizes, intervals or season-level breakdown, and the figures are described from slides. NBA data only. The "one and a half to two times" range is spoken as one comparison across 15 to 20 years; he does not say whether the ratio changed over the period. Do not generalize to college or to other sports, and do not present the balanced-floor story as established.

**Example** — From the talk: a missed above-the-break three, with the shooter already halfway back, against a missed rim-area shot where the defense is often out of position (BJkCqf6Fj2w [07:07], [08:10]).

**Related** — [[framework--frame-findings-with-story-mechanism-and-grain-of-truth]], [[principle--basketball-possession-has-a-third-outcome-not-shooting]].

# The Mid-Range Share Fell, but Stars' Self-Created Mid-Range Shots Held Steady

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") tests "the mid-range game has been lost". He defines mid-range as outside the paint and inside the three-point arc (BJkCqf6Fj2w [08:43]). Part true: the mid-range share "plummeted" while the three-point share rose, which is "unmistakably true" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [08:43], [09:14]). Part not: when people mourn the lost mid-range, he argues they mean players creating their own shot at the top of the key or elbows, not a power forward taking a 17-foot baseline jump shot (BJkCqf6Fj2w [09:14]).
- Unassisted (self-created) mid-range shots "have held basically steady" over time, while assisted ones fell (BJkCqf6Fj2w [09:44]); catch-and-shoot attempts moved from low-value areas toward the rim and the corners (BJkCqf6Fj2w [10:14]).
- For high-usage players, defined arbitrarily as usage 27% or higher, long two-pointers rose from 7% to 11.5% of their made shots over about 15 years, "over 50%" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [10:44]).
- Unassisted above-the-break threes by this group doubled to tripled over four years, driven by a few players; about 340 extra unassisted threes last year versus the 2000 rate, of which two players accounted for 308, "if I did the math correctly" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [11:16], [11:47]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is a redefinition of what "mid-range" means in the complaint, which he calls "star shots" taken by the best players (BJkCqf6Fj2w [09:44]). No mechanism is given for why stars' share held steady.

**When to apply** — As a reminder to split an aggregate trend by who produces the shots (assisted or not, usage group) before accepting a story. Inference: the same split applies to team-level load or testing averages that hide a few athletes who drive the change; at Baylor, check the athlete-level distribution before reading a team trend.

**When NOT to apply** — Supported for the direction of the trends; the numbers were shown on slides the captions do not describe. The 27% usage cutoff is "arbitrary" by his own word, the group is small, and he warns that the unassisted-three rise is driven by two players and the math may be wrong (BJkCqf6Fj2w [11:47]). NBA data only. It does not show these shots are efficient; a questioner raised that and the answer was that the shot clock limits alternatives (BJkCqf6Fj2w [23:25], [23:56]).

**Example** — The talk's: 7% to 11.5% of high-usage players' made shots being long twos (BJkCqf6Fj2w [10:44]).

# Baseball Analogies Break Where a Basketball Possession Can End With No Shot at All

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") says many concepts port from baseball to basketball: rate stats over counting stats, efficiency, and treating the possession or shot like a plate appearance (BJkCqf6Fj2w [12:48], [13:18]). Past a certain level of detail, two differences matter (BJkCqf6Fj2w [13:18], [13:48], [14:18]):
- **No batting order.** In baseball "one through nine hits", but in basketball "there aren't turns"; a hot player can shoot every time down the court.
- **A third outcome.** A baseball plate appearance ends safe or out; a shot is made or missed, but "a very important third possibility" is "not shoot at all". "There's no equivalent of a pass in baseball."
Consequence he draws: "a lot of what we would see as having a shot been contested well means that a player doesn't shoot at all" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18]). He cites the corner three as the example: it is one of the most valuable shots yet a small share of attempts, "because you have to do something right beforehand" and the defense is trying to stop it (BJkCqf6Fj2w [14:48]).

**Why it works** — Stated by the speaker: because a possession has the option of not shooting, the defense's effect shows up in shots not taken, which a shot-level success rate cannot see (BJkCqf6Fj2w [14:18], [15:18]). He gives no data for the corner-three share.

**When to apply** — When importing a metric or model from one sport to another. Inference: ask what the equivalent of "no shot" is in the new sport, an outcome the metric silently drops. At Baylor, the same question applies to any athlete-data measure where non-events (a test not taken, a session not logged) are missing, not zero. Eric's baseline: Eric's SportSmith writing states "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (`2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`, explicit).

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker's conceptual argument and a single example, no data. He calls the whole account "just a theory" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [21:22]). # Defensive Three-Point Percentage Looks Like a Coin Flip, Yet Defenders Affect Shots: "Defending the Three Means Avoiding It"

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") says that, in his view, defensive three-point percentage, at team or individual level, "is not really a thing", because what happens once the shot leaves the offensive player's hands is "out of the defense's hands" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:48], [16:18]). Support: a graph by another writer (caption spelling "Hest Becker") indicating that individual defensive three-point percentage "looks a lot like a coin flip would look" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:18]). He then qualifies it: he is "not saying that it is just luck", only that it looks like it would if it were (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:48]). Where defenders do affect a shot:
- Distance: a shooter four feet from the defender on a catch-and-shoot shoots about 34%, at ten feet about 40% (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:48], [17:18]).
- Fouls: fouling a jump shooter "turns a 35% shot into a 75 or 80% shot" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:18]).
- Late shot clock and end-of-game situations show low three-point percentages "even controlling for all other factors", but he says that style of defense is not available in regular play, because a defender must also stop the drive (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:18], [17:48]).
His conclusion: a catch-and-shoot three below roughly 34% is usually not taken, and "even a 34% three is a 51% effective shot", so "defending the three means avoiding the three entirely" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:48], [18:19]). He uses baseball's batting average on balls in play (BABIP) as the analogy, noting that in baseball the "no control" idea was later "relaxed a fair amount" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18], [15:48]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives a partial mechanism: the contest affects the shot only through distance, fouls and clock context, and most of the defensive effect shows up as shots not taken (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18], [18:19]). The coin-flip comparison itself is shown with a graph by another writer and no detail.

**When to apply** — As a caution against using an outcome rate the defense does not control as a skill metric, and as an example of the risk of reading a flat distribution as "luck". Inference: the same caution applies to any Baylor metric whose variation looks random at the individual level, where one should ask what the measure does not capture before using it to judge a person. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a): "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise."

**When NOT to apply** — Contested within the talk itself: he says the percentage is "not really a thing" and looks like a coin flip, and in the same passage lists real defender effects (distance, fouls, late clock). The coin-flip evidence is a single graph from another writer with no detail shown, and the 34% and 40% figures have no sample or source stated aloud. The caption "worth 50% less" at 20 feet at the end of the talk is unclear (BJkCqf6Fj2w [19:50]) and should not be relied on. NBA only; a statement about one metric, not about defensive skill in general.

**Example** — The talk's: a 34% three is a 51% effective shot, so a defense cannot make such shots unattractive except by preventing them (BJkCqf6Fj2w [18:19]).

**Related** — [[principle--basketball-possession-has-a-third-outcome-not-shooting]], [[claim--four-drivers-of-rising-three-point-rate]].

# Four Drivers of More Threes: Skill, Permission, Downsizing and Catching the Ball Farther Out

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") ends with what he calls "one truth" and then says all of it is "still just a theory" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [18:50], [21:22]). Teams work harder to create threes because a longer jump shot is more valuable than the jump shots already taken. Four factors (BJkCqf6Fj2w [18:50], [19:20], [19:50]):
- **Individual skill development:** players working more on long-distance shooting because the three "is a vital piece to getting playing time" and staying in the league.
- **Permission:** teams encourage and permit players with that skill to step out and shoot.
- **Downsizing:** less time with two traditional big men and more shooters on the floor.
- **Strategy that changes where players catch the ball:** to take a catch-and-shoot three, the ball must be caught outside the arc, so teams changed where players catch it; "worth 50% less" at 20 feet is unclear in the captions (BJkCqf6Fj2w [19:50]).
Evidence for the net effect: perimeter players have long had high three-point rates, but over the last four years power forwards' three-point rate "jumped substantially", most teams play with four shooters and this year more often five (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:20], [20:51]). His summary: "people are stepping further away from the basket" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:51]). In Q&A he adds a limit: there is "probably" a ceiling on how many players have the skill to space the floor (BJkCqf6Fj2w [23:56]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives these as his theory and does not test any one cause. Inference: with four causes named together and no attribution among them, the account cannot say which one mattered most.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when explaining a league-wide strategy shift: ask separately about skill supply, coach permission, roster design and scheme. Inference: Baylor's analogue is any change in practice or testing culture, where individual skill, staff permission, roster mix and process changes may each contribute and should be asked about separately.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker's own theory, with the only data a power-forward rate chart that the captions do not describe. He acknowledges "better theories" may replace his (BJkCqf6Fj2w [21:22]). He declined to answer a question on how teams measure chains of actions and how advanced they are, saying his team's work is private (BJkCqf6Fj2w [22:25], [22:55]). NBA only, through the 2017 All-Star break (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:20]).

**Example** — From the talk: power forwards' three-point rate "jumped substantially" over four years while perimeter players' rates were already high (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:20]).
